label: thm1.1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm1.1} The Riesz transforms satisfy the following properties. 
\begin{itemize}
\item There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for every sequence of non-negative potentials $V_k \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb R^d)$ we  have 
$$ \| \Big(\sum_k | \nabla (-\Delta + V_k)^{- {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}} f_k |^2 \Big)^{\frac{1}{2}} \|_{L^{1,\infty}(\mathbb R^d)} \le C\, \| \Big(\sum_k | f_k |^2\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}} \|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d)}.$$
\item Let $p \in (1, 2]$. Then the family $\{ \nabla (-\Delta + V)^{- {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}}, \, 0 \le V \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb R^d) \}$ is ${\mathcal R}$-bounded on $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$. 
\item Let $p \in (1, 2]$ and $q \in [p, 2]$. Then there exists a positive constant $C$ such that for every sequence of nonnegative potentials $V_k \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb R^d)$ we have
$$ \| \Big(\sum_k | \nabla (-\Delta + V_k)^{- {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}} f_k |^q \Big)^{\frac{1}{q}} \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)} \le C\, \| \Big(\sum_k | f_k |^q\Big)^{\frac{1}{q}} \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}.$$
\end{itemize}

label: cor1.3
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor1.3}
 Suppose that $m$ is supported in $[\frac{1}{2}, 2]$ and satisfies \eqref{eq666} for some $s > \frac{d}{2} +2$. Then there exists a constant $C$ such that for every sequence of non-negative potentials $V_k \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb R^d)$ we  have 
 \[
 \| \Big( \sum_k \sup_{r > 0} |m(r(-\Delta + V_k) ) f_k|^2 \Big)^{\frac{1}{2}} \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)} \le C\,
 \| \Big(\sum_k | f_k |^2\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}} \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)} 
 \]
for $p \in (1, \infty)$.

label: ex1.1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex1.1}
 Consider the following system of independent $N$ evolution equations with nonnegative potentials $V_k$, 
 \[
 \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u_1}{\partial t} = \Delta u_1 - V_1 u_1, \quad u_1(0) = f_1 \\[1ex]
\dfrac{\partial u_2}{\partial t} = \Delta u_2 - V_2 u_2, \quad u_2(0) = f_2\\
\quad \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial u_N}{\partial t} = \Delta u_N - V_N u_N, \quad u_N(0) = f_N.
\end{cases}
\]
 Then for $p \in (1, 2]$ there exists a constant $C$, independent of $V_k$ and of the size $N$ of the system, 
 such that
 \[
 \|  \left(\sum_{k=1}^N | \nabla u_k |^2\right)^ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}} \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)} \le \frac{C}{\sqrt{t}}\, 
 \|  \left(\sum_{k=1}^N | f_k|^2\right)^ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}} \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}.
 \]
 In order to see this we write  $u_k = e^{-t(-\Delta + V_k)}f_k$ and 
 \[
 \sqrt{t} \nabla e^{-t(-\Delta + V_k)}f_k = \nabla (-\Delta + V_k)^{- {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}} (t(-\Delta + V_k))^ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}} e^{-t(-\Delta + V_k)}f_k.
 \]
We apply Theorems~\ref{thm1.1} and \ref{thm1.2}. The first one for the Riesz transform and the second for the multiplier with the function 
 $m_t(\lambda) = \sqrt{t\lambda}\, e^{-t \lambda}$.

title: Notation
body_md:
We use the following classical notation. If $(X, \mu)$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure space, the usual Lebesgue spaces $L^p(X,\mu)$ are often denoted by $L^p(X)$ and their norms by $\| \cdot \|_p$. For a given Banach space $E$, $L^p(X, \mu, E)$ denotes the Bochner $L^p$ space  of functions with  values in $E$. The norm of $E$ will be denoted by $\| \cdot \|_E$. The space of bounded linear operators from $E$ to $F$ is denoted by ${\mathcal L}(E,F)$. For $T \in {\mathcal L}(L^p,L^q)$ we use the notation
 $\| T \|_{p-q}$ for its norm. For a given Hilbert space $H$, we denote by $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_H$ its scalar product.
head: manual

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}(\cite{HO}, Theorem~1.1)
  Let $({X}, \rho, \mu)$ be a metric measure space of homogeneous type,
  let $(E, \| \cdot \|_E)$ and $(F, \| \cdot \|_F)$ be Banach
  spaces and let $p_0, p, q, a \in [1, \infty)$ be such that $p_0 < p \le q$
  where $\frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p_0} -  \frac{1}{a}$. Let 
  $T : L^p({X}, \mu, E) \to L^q({X}, \mu, F)$ be a bounded linear
  operator and suppose that there exists a bounded linear operator $S : L^p({X}, \mu, E) \to 
  L^q({X}, \mu, F)$
  and a family of linear operators
  $(A_r)_{r>0}$ on $L^p({X}, \mu, E)$ such that
\begin{aufziH}
\item \label{thm:main-a} for some sequence $(\omega_j)$ of
  non-negative numbers satisfying
  \( \displaystyle \sum_{j\ge 1} j^n \omega_j < \infty \) and for each
  $f \in L^{p_0}({X}, E)$ with bounded support and each ball $B(x, r)$
  containing its support, we have the off-diagonal bound
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:At-estimate}
    \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{V(x,(j+1)r)} \int_{C_j(x, r)} \bigl\|  (A_r f)(y)  \bigr\|_E^p  \,d\mu(y)\Bigr)^{\frac{1}{p}} \le \frac{\omega_j}{V(x,r)^{\frac{1}{p_0}}}
    \; \|  f  \|_{L^{p_0}({X}, \mu,E)}.
\end{equation}
 
\item there exist  $\delta, W > 0$ such that
\begin{equation} \label{eq:Hoermander-a-condition}  
 \Bigl( \int_{{X} \setminus B(x, (1{+}\delta)r)} \bigl\|  (T - SA_r) f(y)  \bigr\|_F^a\,d\mu(y)\Bigr)^{\frac{1}{a}}  \quad \le \quad W  \,\|  f   \|_{L^{p_0}({X}, \mu,E)}
\end{equation}
for all $x\in {X}$, $r>0$ and
$f \in L^{p_0}({X}, \mu, E)\cap L^\infty({X}, \mu, E)$ supported in
$B(x, r)$.
\end{aufziH}
\medskip\noindent
Then $T: L^{p_0}({X}, \mu,  E) \to L^{a, \infty}({X}, \mu, F)$ is bounded.\\
In the special case that $p_0{=}a{=}1$, the operator $T$ is of weak-type $(1,1)$.
head: environment

label: prop:prop2-1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:prop2-1}
  Let $a \in [1, \infty)$ and $ \delta > 0$. Consider the following
  properties.
\begin{aufzi}
\item \label{prop2-1-1}(Hörmander condition) There exists a constant $W_0$ such that for all $y,  y' \in {X}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:2-1-Ho}
  \int_{\rho(x,y) \ge (1{+}\delta) \rho(y,y')}  \|  \vec{K}_T(x,y) u - \vec{K}_{T}(x,y') u  \|_{F}^a  \, d\mu(x) \le W_0\, \| u \|_E^a \quad{\rm for \ all}\  u \in E.
  \end{equation}
\item \label{prop2-1-2} There exists a family $(A_r)_{r>0}$ of linear
  operators on $L^p({X}, \mu, E)$ which satisfies the off-diagonal
  bound \eqref{eq:At-estimate} and a constant $W_1$ such that
\[
  \sup_{y \in {X}, r >0} \; 
  \int_{\rho(x,y) \ge (1{+}\delta)r} \|  \vec{K}_T(x,y) u - \vec{K}_{TA_r}(x,y) u  \|_{F}^a  \, d\mu(x) \le W_1\, \| u \|_E^a \quad{\rm for \ all}\  u \in E. 
\] 
\item \label{prop2-1-3} There exists  a constant $ W_2 > 0$ such that
\[
 \int_{{X} \setminus B(x, (1{+}\delta)r)} \bigl\|  (T - TA_r)    f(y)  \bigr\|_F^a\,d\mu(y)  \le \quad W_2 \,\| 
    f  \|_{L^{1}({X},\mu,E)}^a
\]
for all $x\in {X}$, $r>0$ and
$f \in L^{1}({X},\mu, E)\cap L^\infty({X},\mu, E)$ supported in
$B(x, r)$.
\end{aufzi}
Then
$\ref{prop2-1-1} \Rightarrow \ref{prop2-1-2} \Rightarrow
\ref{prop2-1-3}$. In particular, conditions \ref{prop2-1-1} and  \ref{prop2-1-2} both imply that the operator $T$ is of weak type $(1, a)$ as soon as 
  $ T : L^p({X}, \mu, E) \to L^q({X}, \mu, F)$ is bounded for some $p$ and $q$ such that $\frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p_0} -  \frac{1}{a}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow closely \cite{HO}, which uses similar ideas as in \cite{Duong-McIntosh}. We prove that
  $\ref{prop2-1-1} \Rightarrow \ref{prop2-1-2}$. Let $u \in E$ and set 
\[
J(x,y) = \|  \vec{K}_T(x,y)u - \vec{K}_{TA_r}(x,y)u  \|_{F}^a  \quad{\rm and} \quad I = \int_{\rho(x,y) \ge (1{+}\delta)r}   J(x,y) \, d\mu(x),
\]
where $A_r$ is the operator defined by the kernel
\[
  \vec{h_r}(z,y) = \frac{\mathbbm 1_{B(y,r)}(z)}{V(y,r)} I_E
\]
in which $I_E$ denotes the identity operator on $E$. Clearly, this kernel has  a Gaussian upper bound and so  \eqref{eq:At-estimate} holds for $p_0 = 1$. The kernel
$\vec{K}_{TA_r}(x,y)$ is then given by the usual composition
formula. Hence
\begin{align*}
J(x,y) = &  \; \|  \int_{\rho(z,y) \le r} [ \vec{K}_T(x,y) - \vec{K}_{T}(x,z)] \vec{h_r}(z,y)u\, d\mu(z)  \|_{F}^a \\
= &  \; \|  \int_{\rho(z,y) \le r} \frac{\mathbbm 1_{B(y,r)}(z)}{V(y,r)} [ \vec{K}_T(x,y)u - \vec{K}_{T}(x,z)u] \, d\mu(z)  \|_{F}^a \\
\le& \; \left( \int_{\rho(z,y) \le r} \|  \vec{K}_T(x,y)u - \vec{K}_{T}(x,z)u \|_{F} \frac{\mathbbm 1_{B(y,r)}(z)}{V(y,r)} \, d\mu(z) \right)^a\\
\le& \;  \int_{\rho(z,y) \le r} \|  \vec{K}_T(x,y) u- \vec{K}_{T}(x,z)u \|_{F}^a \mathbbm 1_{B(y,r)}(z) \, d\mu(z) V(y,r)^{-1}.
\end{align*}
Using Fubini and  \ref{prop2-1-1}, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
I \le& \; \int_{\rho(z,y) \le r} \int_{\rho(x,y) \ge (1+ \delta)d(z,y)}\|  \vec{K}_T(x,y)u - \vec{K}_{T}(x,z)u \|_{F}^a\, d\mu(x)  \mathbbm 1_{B(y,r)}(z) \, d\mu(z) V(y,r)^{-1}\\
  \le& \; W_0\,  \| u \|_E^a  \int_{d(z,y) \le r} \mathbbm 1_{B(y,r)}(z) \, d\mu(z) V(y,r)^{-1} = W_0\,  \| u \|_E^a,
\end{align*}
which is  property \ref{prop2-1-2}. 

\smallskip\noindent Assume now that \ref{prop2-1-2} is satisfied. Let
$f \in L^{1}({X},\mu, E)\cap L^\infty({X},\mu, E)$ with support
contained in a ball $B(x, r)$. Then,
\begin{align*}
    &  \; \Bigl( \int_{{X} \setminus B(x, (1{+}\delta)r)} \bigl\|  (T - TA_r) f(y)  \bigr\|_F^a\,d\mu(y)\Bigr)^{\frac{1}{a}}\\
   =&  \; \Bigl\|  \int_{X}  ( \vec{K}_T(\cdot,z) - \vec{K}_{TA_r}(\cdot,z)) f(z)\, d\mu(z) \Bigr\|_{L^a({X} \setminus B(x, (1{+}\delta)r), \mu , F)}\\
\le &  \; \int_{X}  \bigl\|  ( \vec{K}_T(\cdot,z)f(z) - \vec{K}_{TA_r}(\cdot,z) f(z))\, d\mu(z) \bigr\|_{L^a({X} \setminus B(x, (1{+}\delta)r), \mu ,  F)}\\
=&   \; \int_{{X}} \left( \int_{{X} \setminus B(x, (1{+}\delta)r)} \| \vec{K}_T(y,z)f(z) - \vec{K}_{TA_r}(y,z)f(z) \|_{F}^a\, d\mu(y) \right)^{\tfrac{1}a} \, d\mu(z)\\
\le&   \; W_1^{\tfrac{1}a}\,   \int_{X} \| f(z) \|_{E}\, d\mu(z),
\end{align*}
which  proves  property \ref{prop2-1-3}.\\
 The final statement in the proposition follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us denote by $G(t,x,y) = (4 \pi)^{-\frac{d}{2}}\, t^{-\frac{d}{2}} \exp\{ - \frac{| x- y |^2}{4t} \}$ the Gaussian kernel. Let  $\varphi \in \ell^2$ and $h$ a nonnegative and bounded function  on $\mathbb R^d$. Theorem~\ref{thm3.1} gives for ${\bf f} \in L^1(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2) \cap L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)$, 
$$ | \langle e^{-t\mathcal A} (h {\bf f})(x), \varphi \rangle_{\ell^2} | \le e^{t \Delta} (h \| {\bf f} \|_{\ell^2})(x) \| \varphi \|_{\ell^2}$$
and hence
$$ | \langle \int_{\mathbb R^d}  {\bf p}(t,x,y) {\bf f}(y) h(y)\, dy, \varphi \rangle_{\ell^2} | \le \int_{\mathbb R^d} \| \varphi \|_{\ell^2} G(t,x,y)  \| {\bf f} \|_{\ell^2} (y) h(y)\, dy.$$
Then a simple application of Fubini's theorem implies that 
$$ | \int_{\mathbb R^d}  \langle {\bf p}(t,x,y) {\bf f}(y) , \varphi \rangle_{\ell^2} h(y)\, dy | \le \int_{\mathbb R^d} \| \varphi \|_{\ell^2} G(t,x,y)  \| {\bf f} \|_{\ell^2} (y) h(y)\, dy.$$
Since this is true for all nonnegative $h$, it follows that 
$$ |\langle {\bf p}(t,x,y) {\bf f}(y) , \varphi \rangle_{\ell^2} | \le \| \varphi \|_{\ell^2} G(t,x,y)  \| {\bf f} \|_{\ell^2} (y).$$
This inequality is in the a.e. sense but the null set on which it fails  may depend on $\varphi$. Since $\ell^2$ is separable we apply this to a countable dense set, and then take the union of the corresponding null sets to conclude that  
$$ \| {\bf p}(t,x,y) {\bf f}(y) \|_{\ell^2} \le G(t,x,y)  \| {\bf f} \|_{\ell^2} (y).$$
This latter estimate can be converted into operator norm estimate. To do so, let $\psi \in \ell^2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded domain of $\mathbb R^d$.  Define 
${\bf f} =  \psi \mathbbm 1_\Omega$. Then ${\bf f} \in L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)$ and the previous estimate gives
$$ \| \mathbbm 1_\Omega(y) {\bf p}(t,x,y) \psi  \|_{\ell^2} \le G(t,x,y)  \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}.$$
Since this holds for all $\psi \in \ell^2$ it follows that 
$$\| \mathbbm 1_\Omega(y){\bf p}(t,x,y) \|_{{\mathcal L}(\ell^2)} \le G(t,x,y).$$
This proves the corollary  since $\Omega$ was an arbitrary  domain of $\mathbb R^d$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi, \psi \in \ell^2$ and consider the function
$$F(z) = \langle {\bf p}(z,x,y) \varphi, \psi \rangle_{\ell^2}.$$
Set $z= t+is$, and observe that by self-adjointness $\| e^{-is{\mathcal A}} \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)} \le 1$. Therefore, using $e^{-z{\mathcal A}} = e^{-\frac{t}{2}{\mathcal A}} e^{-is{\mathcal A}} e^{-\frac{t}{2}{\mathcal A}}$ and 
\eqref{eq3.7} we see that $\| e^{-z {\mathcal A}} \|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)-L^\infty(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)} \le C_1\, (\text{Re}\, z)^{-\frac{d}{2}}$. Hence 
$$| F(z) | \le C_1\, (\text{Re}\, z)^{-\frac{d}{2}} \| \varphi \|_{\ell^2} \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}, \quad \text{Re}\, z > 0.$$
The  Gaussian upper bound gives
$$ |F(t)| \le (4 \pi)^{-\frac{d}{2}}\, t^{-\frac{d}{2}} \exp\{ - \frac{| x- y |^2}{4t} \} \| \varphi \|_{\ell^2} \| \psi \|_{\ell^2} \quad t > 0.$$
Now we apply \cite{Ouh05}, Lemma 6.18.

label: lem-grad-p
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-grad-p} Let $\beta \in (0, \frac{1}{6})$. Then there exists a positive constant $C$,  independent of ${\bf V}$,  such that 
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d} \| \partial_{j,x}{\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{\ell^2}^2\,   e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}}\, dx \le C\, t^{-1 - \frac{d}{2}}\, \| u \|_{\ell^2}^2
\]
for all $t > 0$, $y \in \mathbb R^d$ and $u \in \ell^2$.
head: environment

label: eq4.4
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\beta \in (0, \frac{1}{6})$ and set for a fixed $u \in \ell^2$ and $t > 0$
\[ 
I := \sum_{j=1}^d \int_{\mathbb R^d} \| \partial_{j,x}{\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{\ell^2}^2\,   e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}}\, dx.
\]
Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
I &=& \sum_{j=1}^d  \int_{\mathbb R^d} \langle \partial_{j,x}( {\bf p}(t,x,y)u\,  e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}}), \partial_{j,x} {\bf p}(t,x,y)u \rangle_{\ell^2}\, dx\\
&& - \sum_{j=1}^d  \frac{2 \beta}{t} \int_{\mathbb R^d} |x_j - y_j| e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}}  \langle  {\bf p}(t,x,y)u , \partial_{j,x} {\bf p}(t,x,y)u \rangle_{\ell^2}\, dx\\
 &=& I_1 + I_2.
\end{eqnarray*}
Recall that ${\bf V}$ is non-negative and hence we can dominate the first term by using the bilinear form ${\mathfrak a}$ as follows\footnote{we ignore some simple facts such as ${\bf p}(t,\cdot,y)u\, e^{\frac{\beta|\cdot-y|^2}{t}}  \in D({\mathfrak a})$. One can do this by inferring  a sequence $\psi_n$ of $C_c^\infty$ functions which converges pointwise to $1$ and use an approximation argument. See the proof of Theorem~6.19 in \cite{Ouh05}.}
\begin{eqnarray*}
I_1 &\le & {\mathfrak a}( {\bf p}(t,x,y)u, {\bf p}(t,x,y)u\,  e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}})\\
&=&-  \int_{\mathbb R^d} \langle \frac{d}{dt} {\bf p}(t,x,y)u, {\bf p}(t,x,y)u\, e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}} \rangle_{\ell^2}\, dx\\
&\le& \| \frac{d}{dt} {\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)} \|  {\bf p}(t,x,y)u\, e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}} \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)}.
\end{eqnarray*}
Recall that ${\bf p}(t,x,y)$ satisfies the Gaussian upper bound \eqref{eq3.8} and hence, since $\beta < \frac{1}{4}$, ${\bf p}(t,x,y)u\, e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}}$ still has a Gaussian upper bound and hence
\[
\|  {\bf p}(t,\cdot,y)u\, e^{\frac{\beta|\cdot-y|^2}{t}} \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)} \le C_0\,  t^{-\frac{d}{4}} \| u \|_{\ell^2}
\]
with a constant $C_0$ independent of ${\bf V}$. On the other hand,                                                                                                                                                                            
by the semigroup property
\[ 
{\bf p}(t,x,y) = e^{ -\frac{t}{2}{\mathcal A}} {\bf p}( \frac{t}{2},\cdot,y)(x) \quad {\rm and} \ \int_{\mathbb R^d} {\bf p}(t,x,y) {\bf p}(s,x,y)\, dx = {\bf p}(t+s,y,y).
\]
Hence, using again the Gaussian upper bound \eqref{eq3.8}, 
\begin{eqnarray*}
\|  \frac{d}{dt}{\bf p}(t,\cdot,y)u\, e^{\frac{\beta|\cdot-y|^2}{t}} \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)} &=& \|  {\mathcal A} e^{ -\frac{t}{2}{\mathcal A}} {\bf p}( \frac{t}{2},\cdot,y) u \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)}\\
&\le& \frac{C_0'}{t}  \|  {\bf p}( \frac{t}{2},\cdot,y) u \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)}\\
&=&  \frac{C_0'}{t} \sqrt{ \langle {\bf p}( \frac{t}{2},y,y) u, u \rangle_{\ell^2}}\\
&\le&  C_1\,  t^{-\frac{d}{4} -1} \| u \|_{\ell^2}
\end{eqnarray*}
with a constant $C_1$ independent of ${\bf V}$. 
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq4.4}
I_1 \le C_0C_1\,  t^{-\frac{d}{2} -1} \| u \|_{\ell^2}^2.
\end{equation} 
Concerning the second term $I_2$, we first dominate $\frac{|x_j-y_j|}{\sqrt{t}}$ by $e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}}$ (up to a constant) and obtain
\begin{eqnarray*}
I_2 &\le& \frac{C_3}{\sqrt{t}}\,  \sum_{j=1}^d \int_\mathbb R e^{\frac{2\beta|x-y|^2}{t}} \| {\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{\ell^2}\, \| \partial_{j,x}{\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{\ell^2}\, dx\\
&\le& \frac{C_3}{\sqrt{t}}\,  \sum_{j=1}^d \left( \int_\mathbb R e^{\frac{3\beta|x-y|^2}{t}} \| {\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{\ell^2}^2\, dx\right)^{ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}} \left( \int_\mathbb R e^{\frac{\beta|x-y|^2}{t}} \| \partial_{j,x} {\bf p}(t,x,y)u \|_{\ell^2}^2\, dx\right)^{ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
Using again the Gaussian  upper bound \eqref{eq3.8} and the fact that $\beta < \frac{1}{6}$ we can estimate the last term by 
\[ \frac{C_4}{\sqrt{t}}\,  t^{-\frac{d}{4}} \sqrt{I}\, \| u \|_{\ell^2}. 
\]
This together with \eqref{eq4.4}, gives
\[
I \le C_0C_1\,  t^{-\frac{d}{2} -1} \| u \|_{\ell^2}^2 + C_4\,  t^{-\frac{d}{4} - \frac{1}{2}} \sqrt{I}\, \| u \|_{\ell^2}
\]
which implies the estimate in the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(V_n)$ be a sequence of non-negative potentials on $\mathbb R^d$ and each $V_n$ is locally integrable. Let  ${\bf V}$ be  the diagonal operator  whose entries are $V_k, k = 0,1, \cdots$. The vector-valued  Schr\"odinger operator ${\mathcal A}$ acts as a diagonal operator so that for ${\bf f} = (f_k)$, ${\mathcal A}{\bf f} =((-\Delta + V_k)f_k)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm4.1}, the Riesz transform of ${\mathcal A}$ is weak type $(1,1)$ with a bound independent of $(V_k)$ and  this shows  the first assertion. \\
By interpolation with the $L^2(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)$ estimate,  we obtain a  bound on $L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)$ for $p \in (1,2]$ by a constant  independent of $(V_k)$. This means exactly that the set $\{ \nabla(-\Delta + V)^{- {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}}, \ 0 \le V \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb R^d) \}$ is ${\mathcal R}$-bounded on $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$.\\
Finally,  it is clear from Theorem~\ref{thm2.1} that $\nabla{\mathcal A}^{- {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}}$ is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^p)$ with a bound independent of $(V_k)$. By interpolation with the  
$L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)$ case discussed above, we obtain the third  assertion of the theorem.

title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem6.1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem6.1}
Let $s > 0$  and suppose that $m$ is supported in $[0, 1]$. Then
\[
I_\psi := \int_{\mathbb R^d} \| m(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2 (1 + |x-y|)^s \, dx \le C \| m  \|_{W^{\frac{s}{2} + \frac{d}{2} + 1, 2}}^2 
\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2
\]
for all $\psi \in \ell^2$. The constant $C$ is independent of $m$, $y$ and ${\bf V}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $g(\lambda) = m(\sqrt{\lambda}) e^\lambda$. Then 
$$
m(\sqrt{\mathcal A}) =  g(\mathcal A) e^{-\mathcal A}
=  \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_\mathbb R \hat{g}(\xi) e^{-(1 - i \xi)\mathcal A}\, d \xi.
$$
Hence,
\[ 
m(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_\mathbb R \hat{g}(\xi) {\bf p}(1 -i \xi, x,y) \psi\, d \xi.
\]
Therefore,
$$ \sqrt{I_\psi} \le \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_\mathbb R |\hat{g}(\xi) | \| {\bf p}(1 -i \xi, \cdot,y) \psi \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, (1 + |x-y|)^s\, dx, \ell^2)}.$$
Next we estimate $\| {\bf p}(1 -i \xi, \cdot,y) \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d, (1 + |x-y|)^s\, dx, \ell^2)}$. For this, we apply Corollary~\ref{cor3.3} and we obtain 
\begin{eqnarray*}
\int_{\mathbb R^d} \| {\bf p}(1 -i \xi, x,y) \psi \|_{ \ell^2}^2 (1 + |x-y|)^s\, dx
&\le& C^2 \int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{-\frac{|x-y|^2}{4 (1+\xi^2)}} (1 + |x-y|)^s\, dx \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2\\
&\le& C'  \int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{-\frac{|x-y|^2}{8(1+\xi^2)}} (1 + \xi^2)^{\frac{s}{2}}\, dx\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2\\
&\le& C'' (1 + \xi^2)^{\frac{s+d}{2}}\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2.
\end{eqnarray*}
The constant $C''$ is independent of $m$ and ${\bf V}$. Inserting this the definition of $I_\psi$ it follows that by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
\begin{eqnarray*}
\sqrt{I_\psi} &\le& C_1 \int_{\mathbb R^d} |\hat{g}(\xi) | (1 + \xi^2)^{\frac{s+d}{4} +\frac{1}{2}} (1 + \xi^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\, d\xi\,  \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}\\
&\le& C_2 \left( \int_\mathbb R |\hat{g}(\xi) |^2 (1 + \xi^2)^{\frac{s+d}{2} +1}\, d\xi \right)^{ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}} \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}\\
&\le& C_3 \| m  \|_{W^{\frac{s}{2} + \frac{d}{2} + 1, 2}} 
\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}.
\end{eqnarray*}
This finishes the proof of the lemma.
head: environment

label: lem6.2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem6.2}
Let $s > 0$  and suppose that $m$ is supported in $[0, 1]$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^d} \| m(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2 (1 + |x-y|)^s \, dx \le C_\varepsilon \| m  \|_{W^{\frac{s}{2} + \varepsilon, \infty}}^2 
\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2
\]
for all $\psi \in \ell^2$. The constant $C_\epsilon$ is independent of $m$, $y$ and ${\bf V}$.
head: environment

label: lem6.3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem6.3}
Let $s > 0$  and suppose that $m$ is supported  in $[0, r]$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^d} \| m(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2 (1 + r|x-y|)^s \, dx \le C_\varepsilon r^d \| \delta_r m  \|_{W^{\frac{s}{2} + \varepsilon, \infty}}^2 
\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2
\]
for all $\psi \in \ell^2$. The constant $C_\epsilon$ is independent of $m$, $y$ and ${\bf V}$. Here $(\delta_r m)(\lambda) = m(r \lambda)$.
head: environment

label: eq6.1
title: Proof
body_md:
Writing $m(\lambda) = m(\lambda) - m(0) + m(0)$ and the term  $m(0)$ gives $m(0) I_{\ell^2}$ we assume that $m(0) = 0$. Consider a function $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(0, \infty)$ with support contained in $[\frac{1}{4}, 1]$ and such that
$\sum_{n \in \mathbb Z} \varphi(2^{-n} \lambda) = 1$ for all $ \lambda > 0$. Then
\[
m(\lambda) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb Z} m(\lambda) \varphi(2^{-n} \lambda) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb Z} m_n(\lambda)
\]
with $m_n(\lambda) = m(\lambda) \varphi(2^{-n} \lambda)$.  By classical approximation arguments, it is enough to prove that $\sum_{n=-N}^N m_n(\sqrt{\mathcal A})$ is of weak type $(1,1)$ with a bound independent of $N$ (and again of ${\bf V}$). In order to do so, we apply Proposition~\ref{prop:prop2-1}. We prove that for all $\psi \in \ell^2$
\begin{equation}\label{eq6.1}
\int_{| x-y | \ge r} \| \sum_{n=-N}^N 
\left( m_n(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) - e^{-r^2\mathcal A} m_n(\sqrt{\mathcal A})\right) \psi \|_{\ell^2}\, dx \le W_1 \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}
\end{equation}
for some constant $W_1$ independent of $r > 0$, $y \in \mathbb R^d$, and ${\bf V}$.

Set $g_n(\lambda) = m_n(\lambda) (1- e^{-r^2\lambda^2})$ and
\[
I_n(\psi) = \int_{| x-y | \ge r} \| g_n(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi \|_{\ell^2}\, dx.
\]
We start with the obvious inequality
\begin{eqnarray*}
I_n(\psi) \le &&\left( \int_{\mathbb R^d}  \| g_n(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2(1+ 2^n |x-y|)^{2s}\, dx\right)^ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}\\
&& \times  \left(\int_{|x-y| \ge r} (1 + 2^n|x-y|)^{-2s}\, dx \right)^ {{}^{1}\!\!/\!{}_{2}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
By Lemma~\ref{lem6.3} we have exactly as in \cite{DOS} or \cite{Ouh05}
\begin{eqnarray*}
\int_{\mathbb R^d} \| g_n(\sqrt{\mathcal A})(x,y) \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2(1+ 2^n |x-y|)^{2s}\, dx
&\le& C_\varepsilon 2^{nd} \| \delta_{2^n}g_n \|_{W^{s + \varepsilon, \infty}}^2 \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2\\
\vspace{-2cm}&\le& C'_\varepsilon \sup_{t > 0} \| \varphi(\cdot) m(t\cdot) \|_{W^{s + \varepsilon, \infty}}^2 \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}^2
\min(1, r2^n) \| \psi \|_{\ell^2}.
\end{eqnarray*}
On the other hand
\[
\int_{|x-y| \ge r} (1 + 2^n|x-y|)^{-2s}\, dx \le C' 2^{-nd} \min(1, (2^n r)^{d-2s}).
\]
Putting these estimates together yields for $s > \frac{d}{2}$,
\[
\sum_{n =-N}^N I_n(\psi) \le C''_\varepsilon \sup_{t > 0} \| \varphi(\cdot) m(t\cdot) \|_{W^{s + \varepsilon, \infty}}\| \psi \|_{\ell^2}
\]
which gives \eqref{eq6.1}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose the function $m$ satisfies the assumption in the theorem. The first two assertions follow directly from Theorem~\ref{thm6.1} in which we take  ${\bf V}$ to be the diagonal operator  whose entries are $V_k$.

To see the third assertion, observe that  for a given nonnegative potential $V$ on $\mathbb R^d$, the $L^p$-norm of $m(-\Delta +V)$ can be estimated by a constant independent of $V$. This  is a special case of Theorem~\ref{thm6.1}. Therefore, for the diagonal potential ${\bf V}$, $m(\mathcal A): L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^p) \to L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^p)$ is bounded by a constant independent of $(V_k)$. By interpolation with the $L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2)$ estimate given in Theorem~\ref{thm6.1} we obtain the assertion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider again the case where ${\bf V}$ is the diagonal operator with entries $V_k$.  We apply Theorem~\ref{thm6.1} and \cite{DK2}, Corollary~3.5. In the language of \cite{DK2}, $\mathcal A$ admits a  
$W^{s, \infty}$ functional calculus for $s > \frac{d}{2}$. The Sobolev embedding 
$W^{s+ \frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon, 2}$ into $W^{s, \infty}$ shows that $\mathcal A$ has  $W^{\beta, 2}$ functional calculus for $\beta > \frac{d}{2} + \frac{1}{2}$. Then we apply \cite{DK2}, Corollary~3.5 and notice that $\max(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{{\rm type}(L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2))} -
\frac{1}{{\rm cotype}(L^p(\mathbb R^d, \ell^2))}) = \frac{1}{2}$. The implicit constant in \cite{DK2}, Corollary~3.5, is independent of $(V_k)$ since  its dependence on $\mathcal A$ is  mainly through   ${\mathcal R}$-sectoriality estimates.

label: thm-DP
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-DP}
 Let $(X, \mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space and $H$ a separable Hilbert space. Suppose that $T$ is a bounded linear operator from $L^1(X, H)$ into $L^\infty(X,H)$. Then there exists $K: X \times X \to {\mathcal L}(H)$  strongly measurable such that for every ${\bf f} \in L^1(X, H)$
 \[ 
 T{\bf f}(x) = \int_X K(x,y) {\bf f}(y)\, d\mu(y) \quad {\rm a.e.} \, x \in X.
 \]
 In addition, $K$ is bounded and $\operatorname*{ess-sup}_{(x,y) \in X\times X}\| K(x,y) \|_{{\mathcal L}(H)} = \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)}$. The kernel $K$ is unique (up to a null set of $X \times X$).
head: environment

label: App1
title: Proof
body_md:
Take an orthonormal basis $(e_k)$ of $H$ and define the operator
\[
T_{ij} g = \langle T(e_i g), e_j \rangle_H, \quad {\rm for}\ g \in L^1(X).
\]
Clearly, 
$$ \| T_{ij}g \|_{L^\infty(X)} \le \| T(e_ig) \|_{L^\infty(X,H)} \le \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)} \| g \|_{L^1(X)}.$$
By the (scalar) Dunford-Pettis theorem, there exists a measurable bounded function $k_{ij}$ on $X \times X$ such that for every $g \in L^1(X)$
\begin{equation}\label{App1}
 T_{ij} g(x) = \int_X  k_{ij}(x,y) g(y)\, d\mu(y) \quad {\rm a.e.}\ x \in X.
 \end{equation}
 Taking the union over $(i,j)$ of null sets, this equality holds for a.e. $x \in X$ independently of $i, j$. Note also that 
 \begin{equation}\label{App2}
 \| k_{ij} \|_{L^\infty(X\times X)} = \| T_{ij} \|_{L^1(X)\to L^\infty(X)} \le \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)}.
 \end{equation}
We can view $H$ as $\ell^2$ and define $K(x,y)$ as the (infinite) matrix whose entries are $k_{ij}(x,y)$. In order to see that for $(x,y)$ outside a null set $K(x,y)$ defines a bounded operator on $H$ we proceed as follows. Take  $\varphi = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i e_i$ and $\varphi = \sum_{i=1}^M \beta_i e_i$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{App2.2}
\langle K(x,y) \varphi, \psi\rangle_H = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \overline{\beta}_j k_{ij}(x,y)
\end{equation}
is the kernel of the operator $T_{\varphi, \psi}: L^1(X) \to L^\infty(X)$,
\[
T_{\varphi, \psi}g(x) = \langle T(\varphi g)(x),  \psi\rangle_H.
\]
Hence, by \eqref{App2} and again the scalar Dunford-Pettis theorem
\[
| \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \overline{\beta}_j k_{ij}(x,y) | \le \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)}\| \varphi \|_H \| \psi \|_H.
\]
By density and \eqref{App2.2} this implies that
\[
\| K(x,y) \varphi \|_H \le \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)} \| \varphi \|_H
\]
for all $\varphi$ as above. By density again, $K(x,y)$ is a bounded operator on $H$ with norm
\begin{equation}\label{App2.5}
\| K(x,y) \|_{{\mathcal L}(H)} \le \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)} \quad {\rm a.e.} \ (x,y) \in X \times X.
\end{equation}
Note that for  $\varphi = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i e_i$ and
$\varphi = \sum_{i=1}^M \beta_i e_i$, the function 
$$(x,y) \mapsto \langle K(x,y) \varphi, \psi\rangle_H$$
is measurable (as a finite linear combination of measurable functions) and by \eqref{App2.5} and approximation,
this function is measurable for all $\varphi, \psi \in H$. That is, $K(\cdot, \cdot)$ is weakly measurable.  Since $H$ is separable, 
$K(\cdot, \cdot)$ is then strongly measurable by Pettis' theorem. 

Next, for ${\bf f} = \sum_{i=1}^N f_i e_i$ with $f_i \in L^1(X)$ we have
\begin{eqnarray*} 
\langle T{\bf f}(x), e_j \rangle_H &=& \sum_i \langle T{ f_i e_i}(x), e_j \rangle_H
= \sum_i \int_X k_{ij}(x,y) f_i(y) \, d\mu(y)\\
&=& \int_X \langle K(x,y) {\bf f} (x), e_j\rangle_H \, d\mu(y).
\end{eqnarray*}
Hence
\[
 T{\bf f}(x) = \int_X K(x,y) {\bf f}(y)\, d\mu(y) 
 \]
for a.e. $x \in X$. By density and \eqref{App2.5}, this extends to all ${\bf f} \in L^1(X, H)$. The above representation gives
\[ 
|T{\bf f}(x)| \le  \operatorname*{ess-sup}_{(x,y) \in X\times X}\| K(x,y) \|_{{\mathcal L}(H)} \| {\bf f} \|_{L^1(X, H)}
\]
and hence the equality 
\[
\operatorname*{ess-sup}_{(x,y) \in X\times X}\| K(x,y) \|_{{\mathcal L}(H)} = \| T \|_{L^1(X,H)\to L^\infty(X,H)}
\]
is proved. 

The uniqueness of the kernel can be proved as follows. Suppose that for all  ${\bf f}, {\bf g} \in L^1(X,H)$,  
\[ 
\int_X \int_X \langle K(x,y) {\bf f} (y), {\bf g}(x) \rangle_H\, d\mu(y) d\mu(x) = 0.
\]
Applying this to   ${\bf f} = f e_i$ and ${\bf g} = g e_j$, yields 
\[ 
\int_X \int_X f(y) \overline{g(x)} k_{ij}(x,y) d\mu(y) d\mu(x) = 0 \quad {\rm for\  all}\  f, g \in L^1(X).
\]
This gives $k_{ij} (x,y) = 0$ for a.e. $(x,y)$. Taking again the union over $i, j$ of null sets we obtain $K(x,y) = 0$ for a.e. $(x,y) \in X \times X$.
